key_concept: Second-period elements have only four valence orbitals ($ns$ and three $np$, no $d$ orbitals), so their maximum covalency is four, whereas third-period elements can use vacant $3d$ orbitals and exceed four.
steps: Count the valence orbitals. Period-2 elements (Be, B) have $2s + 2p_x + 2p_y + 2p_z$ = 4 valence orbitals and no $2d$ subshell. Period-3 elements (Mg, Al) have $3s$, three $3p$ and five $3d$ orbitals = 9 valence orbitals.
Statement (1): Boron has only 4 valence orbitals, so its maximum covalency is 4, as in $[BF_4]^-$ and $[B(OH)_4]^-$. This is correct.
Statement (2): Beryllium is also in period 2, so it has 4 valence orbitals ($2s$ + three $2p$), not 3. This is incorrect.
Statement (3): Magnesium is in period 3 and can use vacant $3d$ orbitals, so its maximum covalency is greater than 4, i.e. 6 (e.g. $[Mg(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$). This is incorrect.
Statement (4): Aluminium has $3s$, $3p$ and $3d$ orbitals available, giving 9 valence orbitals, not 5. It shows covalency up to 6, as in $[AlF_6]^{3-}$. This is incorrect.
Only statement (1) is correct, which matches the official answer.
final_answer: Option (1): Boron has a maximum covalency of four.
why_not_others: Be has four valence orbitals, not three. Mg and Al, being period-3 elements with vacant $3d$ orbitals, can show covalency up to six (e.g. $[AlF_6]^{3-}$), and Al has nine valence orbitals, not five.
common_trap: Students count only the occupied orbitals (e.g. Be's $2s^2$, or Al's $3s^23p^1$) instead of all available valence orbitals, or they assume Mg, like Be, is limited to a covalency of four.
time_saving_tip: Remember the rule: period 2 means exactly 4 valence orbitals and a maximum covalency of 4, while period 3 has $d$ orbitals and a covalency of up to 6. Option (1) is the only one fitting this rule.
